new_statements.rule_in_words: Alamin (2006) says Laggori has no tone and is a stress language, but gives no placement rule and says stress needs further investigation. This conflicts with Tucker & Bryan 1966 (Daju group incl. Liguri: three tone levels; stress of some importance, not investigated) and with Manfredi 2013 as summarised by Wikipedia (tonal, high and falling tones; Manfredi's own 2022 Laggori data are tone-marked). Dimmendaal 2015 explicitly doubts the stress analysis. No source states where stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Alamin flags stress as uninvestigated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; the sources are noun-morphology and loanword studies, not prosodic descriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern sources describe 'Laggori/Laggorí' (= Liguri proper, lÓgørik), one of the three closely related dialects of the Liguri cluster (Liguri, Saburi, Tallau; Stevenson 1964:111 via Boyeldieu); Alamin 2006 and Manfredi 2013/2015 worked with Laggorí speakers displaced to Khartoum. Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat Shatt and Liguri jointly as 'Eastern Daju' with Shatt-based data. Glottolog logo1261 covers the whole cluster; no separate glottocodes for Saburi/Tallau.

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in the catalog; the only existing statement is Alamin Mubarak 2006 ('There is no tone in Laggori. It is a stress language. The issue of stress needs further investigation.'). Tucker & Bryan differ on tone (three tone levels noted, though no tonal doublets) and agree that stress exists but is uninvestigated; neither gives placement. The T&B statement is group-level, based mainly on Shatt, not a Liguri-specific claim: in every snippet retrieved LIGURI occurs only in the division statement (p. 231), a p. 231 footnote fragment ('.. in LIGURI. Cf. PARANILOTIC, p. 447') and the interrogative table. Access: archive.org item is borrow-only (access-restricted-item true; pdf//hocr all pr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Daju group as a whole (Eastern: Shatt and Liguri; Western: Daju of Darfur/Sila and Njalgulgule; data mainly Stevenson's Shatt), three tone levels have been observed but no tonal minimal pairs found; stress is said to seem important but was not investigated. No placement rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the authors state stress 'has not been fully investigated' and examples are not tone-marked
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's DAJU chapter covers the whole Daju group (Eastern: SHATT and LIGURI; Western: DAJU [Darfur, Sila] and NJALGULGULE) and states that Stevenson's material 'deals mainly with SHATT, from which the majority of examples are consequently taken'; the Tone and Stress statement is thus a group-level remark grounded in Shatt (shat1244), not a description of Liguri/Logorik (logo1261) specifically. Liguri = Laggori = Logorik (ISO liu) per our earlier reading notes.

readall_conflicts: Tucker & Bryan 1966 (Daju group, Shatt-based, p. 232) report three tone levels but no tonal doublets, plus stress of 'some importance' left uninvestigated; Alamin Mubarak 2006 (Laggori, pp. 12-13, snippet already held by the project) says there is no tone and Laggori is a stress language, with stress needing further investigation; Manfredi 2013 as summarised by Wikipedia describes Laggori as tonal (high and falling tones), and Dimmendaal 2015 flags Alamin's stress analysis as needing phonetic investigation. The sources therefore disagree on whether the language is tonal or stress-based, and no source gives a stress-placement rule.
